### 4.1 Discussion

Folate deficiency leads to megaloblastic anemia in both children and adults. This condition

continues to pose a substantial health burden in developing countries, and in underserved

populations, where folate insufficiency persists despite widespread food fortification and routine

supplementation.

A new etiology for folate-deficiency induced megaloblastic anemia

Folate deficiency has been proposed to impair thymidylate synthesis, thereby altering the

dTTP:dUTP ratio1. This imbalance is thought to promote uracil incorporation into DNA, leading

to DNA damage and increased apoptosis of erythroid precursors, ultimately resulting in anemia2.

However, this model has been challenged due to limited molecular evidence for DNA damage or

apoptosis in erythroid progenitors, and no widely accepted alternative mechanism.

Folate deprivation induces metabolic stress that disrupts erythroid differentiation, driving

premature maturation of progenitor cells and reducing their proliferative capacity. This premature

differentiation of progenitor cells limits the number of cell divisions that normally occur before

maturation, resulting in a reduced number of cells within that lineage. We also found that folate

deprivation leads to a transcriptionally regulated increase in cellular heme metabolism. Our results

suggest an etiology that accounts for the decreased erythroid cell numbers and the enlarged,

hemoglobin-rich cells characteristic of megaloblastic anemia. We propose that folate deprivation

is sensed by the cell, activating an erythroid differentiation program through a yet undefined

upstream mechanism. We found that PKC inhibition rescues the differentiation phenotype,

suggesting a possible role in this signaling cascade. Our work also confirmed previously reported

link between AICAR accumulation and PKC signaling, showing a functional connection during


<!-- Page 158 -->


94

differentiation. Through modeling mild folate deficiency in erythroid cells in culture, and profiling

the metabolic consequences, we identified premature and aberrant erythroid differentiation as a

potential mechanistic basis for nutritional megaloblastic anemia.

1CM and nutrient sensing

1CM is a highly conserved metabolic pathway which plays a pivotal role in coupling

nutrient status to gene expression3. Modulation of the translational machinery provides cells with

a rapid mechanism to adjust protein expression in response to environmental factors such as

nutrient availability4. Positioned at the intersection of nucleotide and amino acid metabolism,

translation is directly influenced by 1CM, making this pathway a central regulator of cellular

adaptability and fitness5.

In Ch. 3, we aimed to link folate deprivation induced 1CM-pertubation (inhibited

nucleotide and amino acid biosynthesis) with the regulation of the ribosome. We found that

culturing K562 cells in folate-deplete media perturbs 1CM metabolism, leading to changes in

purine synthesis (Ch. 2), and downstream to potential changes in ribosomes and translation (Ch.

3). We found that KO of mTORC1 genes affects cellular fitness in K562 cells cultured in low-

folate media via our CRISPR screen. This supports a connection between 1CM perturbation via

folate depletion and mTORC1 mediated adaptation of the cell. We also found that changes to

translation occurred in genes related to glycosylation, known to have a role in ribosomal

regulation, and histones, which regulate ribosomal gene transcription by modifying chromatin

structure to control accessibility to ribosomal DNA genes.

There are many open questions remaining in terms of the cellular response and adaptation

to 1CM perturbation, particularly in the context of cellular fitness. Through our studies, we


<!-- Page 159 -->


95

identified many potential connections for exploring the regulation of cellular fitness during folate

deprivation at the level of the ribosome and translation.

Intersections between folate metabolism and cellular stress responses

Our studies revealed many potential connections between the cellular response to folate

depletion and various stress responses. We can assess the role of the heat shock response (HSR),

integrated stress response (ISR), unfolded protein response (UPR), and the DNA damage response

(DDR). Folate is essential for the maintenance of healthy cells, and future work could reveal a

broad impact of folate scarcity on cellular stress. Importantly, our experiments were completed

primarily in erythroid cells (K562), and future studies could include expanding to other cell types

to further assess the impact of folate deprivation on overall human cellular biology.

The heat-shock response is induced by heat, but also by other environmental factors,

including nutrient depletion, as this stress response helps maintain proteostasis6. In the CRISPR

screen, HSF2 and HSF4 KO improves cell survival in low folate. HSF2 and HSF4 are essential

for development and differentiation processes. Moreover, KO of HSPA8 (Hsp70 isoform) resulted

in improved cell survival in low folate. This isoform is typically constitutively expressed. This is

an interesting connection because the encoded protein is crucial for maintaining proteostasis since

it is involved in protein folding, trafficking, and degradation. It is also a key component of

chaperone-mediated autophagy, where it binds to proteins and transports for lysosomal

degradation7. Additionally in the CRISPR screen, the KO of HSPA1A and HSPA1B (highly

inducible Hsp70 isoforms), resulted in decreased cell survival in low folate. Hsp70 is necessary

for the folding of new synthesized and misfolded proteins, and also facilitates the degradation of

damaged proteins by the ubiquitin-mediated proteasomal system8. Interestingly, it has also been


<!-- Page 160 -->


96

shown that Hsp70 phosphorylation exerts anti-apoptotic properties upon serum starvation in

hepatocellular carcinoma. This stress response is known to regulation stress tolerance, proteostasis,

and coordination of the cell between the HSR and autophagy9. These preliminary results may

indicate a broad coordination of the cell to ameliorate proteotoxicity induced by folate deprivation.

Nutrient deprivation, in particular amino acid deficiency, triggers the ISR. Therefore, we

could expect that folate deprivation may induce the ISR. From the CRISPR screen, we do not see

major changes in cell survival in low folate when the following ISR biomarkers are KO: GDF15,

PSME4, SQSTM1, ATF4. However, assessing these biomarkers via the screen does not give a

complete picture. Since the ISR works through the phosphorylation of EIF2a (resulting in a

decrease in global protein synthesis, to conserve energy and reduce further accumulation of

misfolded proteins), it would be best to investigate this pathway more directly through western

blotting. We could assess EIF2a phosphorylation, ATF4, CHOP, and PERK to give us a better

picture of ISR activation.

Nutrient deprivation (for example glutamine or glucose starvation) can induced the DDR,

sensing DNA damage and initiating repair mechanisms. However, our results in Chapter 2 show

that low folate depletion does not induce the DDR as shown through no significant increase in

phosphorylated CHK1 and no significant increase in γH2AX by Day 4 of folate depletion. KO

biomarkers of the DDR do not result in major increases or decreases in cell survival in our low

folate CRISPR screen.

Inhibiting 1CM by targeting SHMT1 or MTHFD2 is shown to induce cell stress by the

depletion of purines and glycine- which we show in chapter 2 also occurs through 1CM

perturbation by folate depletion. This was shown to induce the UPR in glioblastoma10 as well as

hepatocellular carcinoma cells11 through the upregulation of ATF4, but the direct link has not been


<!-- Page 161 -->


97

shown in K562. Our CRISPR results do not show a connection between the UPR and survival of

cells in low folate, however a better technique for assessing this connection would be qPCR or

western blotting to determine changes in mRNA and protein levels of UPR markers in cell

deprived of folate.

Cell-type dependence of stress responses to folate deprivation

We expect stress responses and genetic dependencies under low folate to be partly cell-type

specific and partly conserved. For example, we observe increased heme synthesis specifically in

erythroid cells (Chapter 2), which reflects their uniquely high demand for hemoglobin production

and coordinated erythroid differentiation programs. K562 cells are rapidly proliferating and retain

the capacity for erythroid differentiation, including inducible globin expression and active iron

metabolism, though these features are less pronounced than in primary erythroid cells. All of these

characteristics may shape how folate limitation is sensed and buffered.

At the same time, some responses to low folate are likely shared across cell types, particularly

those linked to core metabolic stress. For instance, our data show depletion of purine pools

(Chapter 2), which is expected to impact nucleotide balance, replication, and growth signaling.

Consistent with prior work by Hoxhaj et al., such metabolic stress may converge on nutrient-

sensing pathways like mTOR, which broadly regulate anabolic demand in response to metabolite

availability12.

Thus, while erythroid-specific features (like heme synthesis, extreme translational demand)

may drive unique dependencies, we expect key aspects of the response (such as nucleotide

depletion and nutrient sensing) to generalize across cell types.

Analysis of published UFMylation interaction datasets suggests a link between UFMylation and

cellular metabolic regulation

As an emerging PTM with diverse roles, recent high-throughput studies have mapped the

UFMylation interactome using IP-MS, identifying 337, 706, and 887 potential interactors13-15. A

previous lab member, Adam Maynard, compared these datasets to identify shared targets. ACLY,

ARL1, and NDUFA4 were the only three proteins in common across all three studies. None of

these have yet been confirmed as bona fide UFMylation substrates. Notably, ACLY and NDUFA4

are both linked to cellular metabolism. ATP citrate lyase (ACLY) is a cytosolic enzyme that

converts citrate and CoA into acetyl-CoA and oxaloacetate. It acts as a crucial bridge between

carbohydrate metabolism and lipogenesis, providing acetyl-CoA for fatty acid synthesis,

cholesterol biosynthesis, and histone acetylation. NDUFA4 is a subunit of complex IV of the

mammalian electron transport chain16. Although there are only 3 proteins shared across all three

published data sets, there are many more potential metabolic targets of UFMylation to explore.

Therapeutic opportunities at the intersection of UFMylation and folate metabolism

Our findings suggest a potential clinical implication for antifolate response and resistance.

Because inactivation of the UFMylation pathway confers a proliferative advantage under low-

folate conditions, tumors with reduced UFMylation activity may be relatively more tolerant of

folate stress and could therefore be less sensitive to antifolates such as methotrexate.

UFL1 promotes tumor growth in pancreatic cancer by enhancing the UFMylation of PARP1,

which stabilizes it and suppresses the DDR17. However, in prostate cancer18, liver cancer (HCC)

19, and CRC20, reduced UFMylation, particularly through the loss of the enzyme UFL1, promotes

cancer progression, metastasis, and immune evasion.


<!-- Page 163 -->


99

This raises the possibility that UFMylation status could serve as a biomarker for antifolate

response, although that remains to be tested directly. Methotrexate works by inhibiting DHFR and

blocking folate-dependent nucleotide synthesis. It is already used to treat several malignancies,

those of hematologic origin, like leukemias and lymphomas, as well as osteosarcoma, breast

cancer, head and neck cancer, and gestational trophoblastic diseases (such as choriocarcinoma).

Our data also raise the possibility that tumors with high anabolic demand, including some

mTOR-activated tumors, may be vulnerable to folate limitation, since purine depletion is expected

to constrain mTOR-linked growth programs. Some related work has shown that inhibition of

folate-mediated 1CM can suppress mTORC1 signaling and promote leukemic differentiation21.

The first questions to address about how inactivating UFMylation gives cells a growth

advantage under low folate are mechanistic: Does UFMylation loss alter methotrexate sensitivity,

and is this effect seen across multiple cell or cancer types or only in specific lineages? Therefore,

the most informative next studies would be cell-line panels and xenograft or genetically engineered

mouse models in which folate intake can be controlled. Those experiments will test whether

UFMylation-deficient tumors are resistant to antifolates, whether mTOR activation predicts

sensitivity, and whether dietary folate modifies treatment response. If those preclinical studies are

convincing, that would justify further planning towards a biomarker-driven clinical trial.

Next steps and caveats in clonal UFM1 knockout K562 cells

In the future, we plan to continue experiments using the clonal KOs of UFM1 in K562. First,

we would perform proliferation assays to measure cell doubling times under low folate conditions.

Based on the screen, we expect knockout cells to survive better than wild-type cells. However, the

screen was conducted in large volumes over ~14 doublings, whereas our standard experiments are


<!-- Page 164 -->


100

performed in smaller volumes (5-25 mL, most typically ~10 mL). Cell behavior can vary with

culture conditions as cells sense their environment and each other, so even at the same cell density,

differences in volume can influence growth and phenotype.

In addition, the response to low folate appears to be time-dependent. We observe distinct

changes at early versus later time points (Chapter 2), suggesting that cells adapt over time.

Furthermore, single-cell clones often adopt unexpected mutations. They are selected for being able

to grow from a single cell into a clonal population, an abnormal condition for cells. Often, these

cells will behave differently than a WT or KO population that is heterogenous.  Therefore, we

might expect that they may adapt differently in response to low folate than the cells used for the

screen.

A natural next step in clonal UFM1 knockout K562 cells would be to perform glycomics and

proteomics under low folate conditions. Glycomics is especially interesting because recent work

from a post-doc in the lab, Peng Wang, showed that folate depletion can alter glycan structures,

and also induces the UPR in T cells.  T cells require a surface glycocalyx for development,

activation, proliferation, and differentiation22. However, the glycocalyx covers all cells (the

glycans are attached to proteins and lipids) and acts as a critical molecular interface for cell

identification, signaling, adhesion, and protection. There is a known association between

glycosylation and the UPR23, but the connection with folate depletion is not yet published.

This is relevant because our RNAseq also suggested differential regulation of genes connected

to ER stress and protein homeostasis under low folate conditions. Testing whether UFM1 KO

changes glycosylation patterns or UPR activation could help connect the low-folate phenotype to

these specific stress-response pathways.

Lessons learned and considerations for future studies

Our approach to this project was to begin by investigating the major known substrate of

UFMylation based on the literature, RPL26. This was a limiting approach because we did not know

whether RPL26 was the main substrate of UFMylation in our system and did not know what else

might be UFMylated in K562 in low folate. Since we now have data showing that UFMylation of

RPL26 might not be a major target in our system, we can move on to find other potential targets.

A suggested approach moving forward could be to cross reference UFMylation proteomics data

and our CRISPR or RNASeq data sets to find new UFMylation candidates until we can perform

our own proteomics experiments.

This is an exciting new chapter for this project, as there are many potential connections to

investigate, and will lead to a better understanding of the link between UFMylation and folate

metabolism.
